content: The recommendation for the use of diagnostic tools is based on evidence of diagnostic accuracy in respiratory samples obtained from adults presenting with clinical signs and symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). This recommendation also applies to individuals living with HIV (PLHIV), as the studies reviewed included varying proportions of such individuals. However, the performance of these tools on smear-negative samples was only evaluated for TB detection and not for rifampicin (RIF) or isoniazid (INH) resistance. Additionally, data stratified by HIV status were not available. The recommendation extends to adolescents and children, with the data generalized from adult studies. It is important to note that indeterminate results are more likely to occur in children with paucibacillary TB disease. The use of these diagnostic tools for extrapulmonary TB or testing on non-sputum samples was not considered due to limited data on the diagnostic accuracy of these technologies in such contexts. The Roche cobas MTB and cobas MTB-RIF/INH assays demonstrate strong performance for diagnosing TB and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) when compared to culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). These assays are capable of detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and resistance to RIF and INH by targeting specific genetic regions, including the rpoB gene for RIF resistance and the inhA promoter region and katG gene for INH resistance. Results for the first 96 samples are generated within three hours, with subsequent results released in 90-minute intervals. The cobas 6800/8800 systems, which automate DNA extraction and real-time PCR with fluorescence detection, are used for these assays. These systems can process up to 384 tests per 8-hour workday (cobas 6800) or 1056 tests per 8-hour workday (cobas 8800). The instruments require weekly maintenance, and any observed contamination or droplet leakage should prompt immediate contact with Roche’s service organization. The cobas MTB kit and associated reagents must be stored at 2–8°C and used within specified timeframes once opened. Sputum samples for testing can be stored at 2–35°C for up to three days or at 2–8°C for up to seven days. The assays are designed for use in laboratories with adequate infrastructure to support molecular workflows, including separate spaces for sample preparation and amplification. The FluoroType MTB and FluoroType MTBDR assays, developed by Bruker-Hain Life Sciences, are also effective for diagnosing TB and detecting RIF and INH resistance. These assays utilize high-resolution melt analysis and light-on/light-off chemistry to detect MTBC and resistance-associated mutations. The assays differentiate between high-level and low-level INH resistance and automatically report specific mutations using FluoroSoftware. Results are available within three hours, and the assays can process 12 samples per run on the FluoroCycler 12 or 96 samples per run on the FluoroCycler XT. Both the Roche and Bruker-Hain assays are classified as moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) by the World Health Organization (WHO). They are recommended for use in individuals with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB for the detection of TB, RIF resistance, and INH resistance, as an alternative to culture and phenotypic DST. Quality assurance systems and regular validation of these assays are essential to ensure accuracy and precision, particularly for detecting drug resistance. Laboratory technicians must be fully trained in the automated processes of these systems, including DNA extraction, amplification, fluorescence detection, and result interpretation. Training should also cover troubleshooting, maintenance, and the review of resistance results for all included drugs. Additionally, laboratories should implement contamination control measures and include positive and negative controls in each run to validate results.
